72	    ABSTRACT                                                                   ARTICLE HISTORY
73	    There is a growing interest in the analysis of diﬀerent methods for        Received 7 March 2019
74	    monitor fatigue during resistance training sessions. This study            Accepted 1 July 2019
75	    aimed to (1) analyse the relationships between the percentage of           KEYWORDS
76	    performed repetitions with respect to the maximum possible                 Velocity-based training;
77	    number (%REP), RPE and magnitude of velocity loss (VL), and (2)            subjective scale; level of
78	    examine whether a multiple regression analysis with the RPE and            eﬀort; exercise prescription
79	    VL as predictor variables could improve the goodness of ﬁt to
80	    predict %REP in the bench press exercise performed in a Smith
81	    machine. Seven men performed a repetition maximum test, on 3
82	    separate testing sessions, against 3 diﬀerent absolute loads based
83	    on a target mean velocity (MV) according to an individual load-
84	    velocity proﬁle (≈1.00, ≈0.70, and ≈0.50 m/s). MV, VL, %REP and
85	    RPE were collected and used for analysis. Based upon quadratic
86	    polynomial regression analysis strong relationships were reported
87	    between the RPE and %REP (r2 = 0.89 and SEE = 9.85%) and
88	    between the VL and %REP (r2 = 0.91 and SEE = 9.85%). Multiple
89	    regression analysis with the RPE and VL as predictor variables
90	    improved the goodness of ﬁt (r2 = 0.94 and SEE = 7.18%) of the
91	    model to predict %REP. These results suggest that both RPE and
92	    VL are useful variables to accurately estimate %REP in the bench
93	    press exercise.
94	
95	
96	
97	Introduction
98	Resistance training has been shown to be a key factor for improving health, body
99	aesthetics and athletic performance (Balshaw et al., 2017; Folland & Williams, 2007;
100	Suchomel, Nimphius, & Stone, 2016). However, coaches and sport professionals require
101	an adequate control of the diﬀerent training variables (e.g., intensity, volume, move-
102	ment velocity, rest periods, etc.) in order to design an eﬀective resistance training
103	program (Kraemer & Ratamess, 2004). Among these training variables, the training
104	intensity and volume seems to be the most important factors impacting the athlete’s
105	neuromuscular adaptations (Campos et al., 2002; Gonzalez-Badillo, Yanez-Garcia,
106	Mora-Custodio, & Rodriguez-Rosell, 2017; Munoz-Lopez, Marchante, Cano-Ruiz,
107	Chicharro, & Balsalobre-Fernandez, 2017).
108	
109	CONTACT Carlos Balsalobre-Fernández              carlos.balsalobre@uam.es
110	© 2019 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
111	 42      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.
112	
113	
114	    Training intensity has traditionally been based on percentage of the one-repetition
115	maximum (%1RM) or on the maximum number of repetitions that can be performed
116	against a submaximal load (Kraemer & Ratamess, 2004; Sakamoto, Sinclair, & Naito,
117	2016). More recently, is has been suggested that movement velocity may be an appro-
118	priate way to control training intensity (González-Badillo & Sánchez-Medina, 2010;
119	Jidovtseﬀ, Harris, Crielaard, & Cronin, 2011; Pareja-Blanco et al., 2017). Previous
120	studies have observed a strong and stable relationship between movement velocity
121	and the relative load (%1RM) in a variety of resistance training exercises, mostly
122	performed in Smith machines (Conceição et al., 2016; García-Ramos, Pestaña-Melero,
123	Pérez-Castilla, Rojas, & Haﬀ, 2018a; Munoz-Lopez et al., 2017; Pérez-Castilla,
124	García-Ramos, Padial, Morales-Artacho, & Feriche, 2017). Velocity-based training has
125	therefore gained popularity in the ﬁeld of strength and conditioning due to the
126	proliferation of and advancements in sports technology (i.e. linear transducers, accel-
127	erometers, or mobile applications) that allow for the accurate measurement of move-
128	ment velocity (Balsalobre-Fernandez et al., 2017; Banyard, Nosaka, Sato, & Haﬀ, 2017;
129	Pérez-Castilla, Piepoli, Delgado-García, Garrido-Blanca, & García-Ramos, 2019).
130	However, many of these devices are not able to be practically used within the strength
131	and conditioning environment and are often not aﬀordable, which limits their ability to
132	be used by many strength and conditioning professionals (Pérez-Castilla et al., 2019).
133	    An alternative approach to monitor resistance training intensity based on the
134	psycho-physiological response of the organism is the ‘rating of perceived exertion’
135	(RPE) (Day, McGuigan, Brice, & Foster, 2004; Eston & Evans, 2009; Gearhart,
136	Lagally, Riechman, Andrews, & Robertson, 2009). According to this, the psychologi-
137	cal/environmental information provokes a subjective perception for a given stimulus
138	(Borg, 1990). The scales commonly used to collect RPE are the Borg (Borg, 1990) or
139	OMNI-RES (Robertson et al., 2003) scales. The RPE has been shown to be a useful tool
140	for predicting the relative load (%1RM) (Day et al., 2004; Eston & Evans, 2009;
141	Gearhart et al., 2009). However, the relationship between the RPE and resistance
142	training intensity may be questionated when performing sets to voiluture failure due
143	to the induced fatigue (Vasquez et al., 2013). Previous investigations have found high
144	relationship between the RPE, %RM, and MV (Bautista, Chirosa, Robinson, Chirosa, &
145	Martinez, 2016; Naclerio & Larumbe-Zabala, 2016). Also, a novel scale in which RPE
146	was based on the number of ‘repetitions in reserve’ (i.e., number of repetitions left in
147	reserve before reaching muscular failure in a training set; RIR) has been developed
148	(Zourdos et al., 2016). More importantly, a recent study by Balsalobre-Fernández,
149	Muñoz-López, Marchante, and García-Ramos (2018) observed that combining RPE,
150	RIR and movement velocity improves the capabilities of traditional load-velocity
151	relationships to predict relative loads (%RM). Therefore, it is well documented in
152	scientiﬁc literature the feasibility of RPE scales to prescribe and monitor training load
153	according to athlete’s subjective perception.
154	    Of special note, is that training intensity in isolation is an inadequate predictor of
155	training adaptation if training volume is not taken into account (Gonzalez-Badillo et al.,
156	2017). It has been widely argued in the scientiﬁc literature that training to muscular
157	failure (i.e., performing the maximum number of repetitions possible with a given
158	relative load) is unnecessary for maximising athletic performance (Davies, Orr, Halaki,
159	& Hackett, 2016; Izquierdo et al., 2006). Velocity loss (VL) has been recently proposed
160	                                                                 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        43
161	
162	
163	as a precise and non-invasive variable to monitor the actual degree or level of eﬀort
164	incurred during resistance training (Sánchez-Medina & González-Badillo, 2011).
165	Previous studies have reported a strong relationship between the relative VL in
166	a training set and the percentage of performed repetitions with respect to the maximum
167	possible number that can be completed (%REP) in the bench press and pull-up
168	exercises in a smith machine (Gonzalez-Badillo et al., 2017; Sanchez-Moreno,
169	Rodriguez-Rosell, Pareja-Blanco, Mora-Custodio, & Gonzalez-Badillo, 2017). By mon-
170	itoring repetition velocity can be accurately estimated with the %RPE (or RIR) when
171	a given percentage of VL is achieved during a training set. However, no known studies
172	have analysed whether the subjective RPE scale is able to estimate the %RPE with
173	similar precision to that seen with the VL method. It also remains unknown whether
174	incorporating the RPE along with VL has additional predication capabilities to mon-
175	itoring %RPE.
176	   In line with the aforementioned considerations, the objectives of the present study
177	were to (1) analyse the relationships between the %REP, RPE and VL, and (2) examine
178	whether a multiple regression analysis with the RPE and VL as predictor variables could
179	improve the precision of the prediction of the %REP in the bench press exercise
180	performed in a Smith machine. We hypothesised that (1) no diﬀerence would be
181	observed between the RPE and VL in the precision of the prediction of %REP, (2)
182	a more precise estimation of the %RPE would be obtained using RPE and VL as
183	predictor variables.
184	
185	
186	Methods
187	Participants
188	The sample size was determined based on previous studies (Sreckovic et al., 2015;
189	Zivkovic, Djuric, Cuk, Suzovic, & Jaric, 2017), which calculated that a sample size
190	between 3 and 12 participants was needed to detect diﬀerences on mechanical para-
191	meters observed from the loaded bench press executions with a signiﬁcant level of
192	p < 0.005 and desired statistical at 0.8. Therefore, we recruited 7 physically active men
193	(age: 22.9 ± 1.9 years; body mass: 77.8 ± 11.7 kg; height: 1.76 ± 0.68 m) volunteered to
194	participate in this study. Participants had at least 1 year of resistance training experience
195	and a bench press 1RM of 83.6 ± 16.4 kg (1.08 ± 0.20 kg/kg body mass). No physical
196	limitations, health problems or musculoskeletal injuries that could compromise tested
197	performance were reported. None of the participants were taking drugs, medications or
198	other substances that could alter their physical performance. Participants were
199	informed of the study procedures and signed a written informed consent form prior
200	to initiating the study. The study protocol adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of
201	Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of
202	Granada.
203	
204	
205	Experimental design
206	A cross-sectional study was designed to examine the RPE-%REP-VL relationships in
207	the bench press exercise. Participant undertook 3 testing session, at the same time of
208	 44      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.
209	
210	
211	the day for each participant, separated by 72–96 hours of rest between them. In each
212	testing session, participants completed a repetition maximum test against an external
213	load based on a target mean velocity (MV) according to previously established indivi-
214	dual load-velocity proﬁle (≈1.00, ≈0.70, and ≈0.50 m/s). The individual load-velocity
215	relationship was was determined based upon the completion of a standardized incre-
216	mental load testing until a 1RM has been achieved (García-Ramos et al., 2018a). During
217	the repeptition maximum test, the RPE scale was inmediately shown to the participants
218	and they were asked to verbally rating the RPE value during each analysis interval
219	previously established (see above for further details). The main variables analysed were:
220	1) mean velocity (MV) of each repetition; 2) MV of the fastest repetition (MVBEST)
221	during the repetition maximum test; 3) MV of the last repetition (MVLAST) during the
222	repetition maximum test; 4) velocity loss (VL) over each analysis interval calculated as
223	100*(MVBEST—MV/MVBEST); 5) percentage of repetitions completed (%REP) with
224	respect to the maximum possible number over each analysis interval; and 6) rating of
225	perceived exertion (RPE) verbally reported over each analysis interval.
226	
227	
228	Testing procedures
229	Familiarisation and initial measures
230	In the 2 weeks prior to the study, participants performed 2 familiarisation sessions,
231	separated by 7 days, to ensure a proper technique during the bench press exercise and
232	familiarise participants with Borg’s RPE (1–10) scale (Borg, 1990). In the ﬁrst familiar-
233	isation session, the anthropometric measures (height and body mass) were taken and
234	then participants carried out a standard incremental loading test to determine the
235	individual load-velocity proﬁle (García-Ramos, Pestaña-Melero, Pérez-Castilla, Rojas,
236	& Haﬀ, 2018b). In the second familiarisation session, participants performed several
237	warm-up sets of 3–8 repetitions with diﬀerent external loads and, subsequently, had to
238	verbally report the RPE value after each set. Thereafter, they carried out a repetition
239	maximum test against an external load based on a target MV of ≈0.70 m/s according to
240	the previously established individual load-velocity proﬁle in order to experience
241	a maximum eﬀort (i.e., RPE 10).
242	
243	Load-velocity proﬁle determination
244	Before the commencement of the load-velocity test, participants performed
245	a standardised warm-up consisting of 5 min of joint mobility, followed by 2 sets of
246	10 and 8 repetitions (interspaced with 2 min rest) with an external load of 20 and 30 kg
247	respectively. After warming up, the individual load-velocity relationship was deter-
248	mined by means of a standard incremental loading test performed in a Smith machine
249	(Technogym, Barcelona, Spain) (García-Ramos et al., 2018a). The initial external load
250	of the incremental loading test was set at 20 kg. Thereafter, the load was progressively
251	increased in 10 kg increments until the MV was lower than 0.50 m/s. From that
252	moment, the load was progressively increased in steps of 5 to 2.5 kg until the 1RM
253	strength was achieved. For the lighter loads (MV ≥ 0.80 m/s), 3 repetitions were
254	performed at each load, 2 for medium loads (0.80 m/s > MV ≥ 0.5 m/s), and only 1
255	for the heavier loads (MV < 0.5 m/s). Participants were verbally asked to provide a RPE
256	value after each load lifted in order to familiarise them with this RPE scale.
257	                                                               SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       45
258	
259	
260	   The bench press technique involved the participants laying supine on ﬂat bench,
261	with their feet fully supported on the ﬂoor and their hands placed on the bar with a self-
262	selected grip-width, which was slightly wider than shoulder width. The self-selected grip
263	width was individually measured and kept constant throughout all testing sessions. The
264	position on the bench was individually adjusted with the vertical projection of the bar
265	corresponding with the participant’s mid line of the chest. Participants were required to
266	lower the bar in a controlled manner until contacting their chest. After maintaining
267	a momentary pause for ≈1–1.5 s, they performed a purely concentric action at the
268	maximum possible velocity. The momentary pause between phases was imposed in
269	order to minimise the eﬀect of the stretch-shortening cycle and the contribution of
270	elastic energy to the movement as proposed previously (Pareja-Blanco et al., 2017).
271	
272	Repetition maximum test
273	Participants completed a standardised warm-up consisted of 5 min of joint mobility,
274	followed by 4 sets of 10 repetitions against 20 kg, 5 repetitions against 30 kg, 5
275	repetitions against 40 kg and 2 repetitions against 50 kg (interspaced with 2 min
276	rest). If the participant reported a higher 1RM than 80 kg, an additional set of 2
277	repetitions against 60 kg was completed. Afterward, participants performed
278	a repetition maximum test based on completing the maximum number of possible
279	repetitions with a submaximal load previously determined according to the individual
280	load-velocity proﬁle. Speciﬁcally, the absolute loads (kg) were established based on
281	a target MV reached at the ﬁrst 1–3 repetitions (usually the fastest) during each
282	repetition maximum test: load 1 = ≈1.00 m/s, load 2 = ≈0.70 m/s, and load
283	3 = ≈0.50 m/s. The repetition maximum test ended when participants were unable to
284	perform a repetition with a proper technique or when a completed range of motion was
285	not reached (Pérez-Castilla, Suzovic, Domanovic, Fernandes, & García-Ramos, 2019).
286	A pause of 2 s. was imposed between the eccentric and concentric phases of each
287	repetition. During each repetition maximum test, the RPE value was inmediately
288	requested from the participant in pre-established analysis intervals: every 5, 3 and 2
289	repetitions during the load 1 (≈1.00 m/s), 2 (≈0.70 m/s), and 3 (≈0.50 m/s), respectively.
290	
291	Measurement equipment and data analysis
292	Anthropometric variables (height and body mass) were measured with a digital stadi-
293	ometer with scale (SECA 220, SECA, Germany). A Smith machine (Technogym,
294	Barcelona, Spain) was used for all tests. An isoinertial dynamometer (ChronojumpTH
295	Boscosystem, Barcelona, Spain), which consists of a cable-extension linear position
296	transducer attached to the bar interfaced with a personal computer at a sampling rate
297	of 1,000 Hz, was used for mechanical measurements. Speciﬁcally MV, which is deter-
298	mined by the diﬀerentiation of the displacement data with respect to time, was auto-
299	matically calculated by the custom software v.1.8.1–54. Reliability and validity of this
300	device has been previously reported else where (Pérez-Castilla et al., 2019). A visual
301	presentation of Borg’s RPE scale (1–10) was used throughout testing.
302	
303	Statistical analyses
304	Descriptive data are presented as means, standard deviations (SD) and coeﬃcients of
305	variation (CV) with the corresponding 95% conﬁdence intervals (CI). The distribution
306	 46      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.
307	
308	
309	of the variables was analysed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests. The non-parametric
310	Kruskal-Wallis H tests were used to compare dependent variables between the repeti-
311	tion maximum tests. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to identify the source of any
312	signiﬁcant diﬀerence. Quadratic polynomial regression models were used to examine
313	the relationship between %REP, RPE and VL. The goodness of ﬁt was assessed by the
314	Pearson’s multivariate coeﬃcient of determination (r2) and the standard error of the
315	estimate (SEE). Multiple regression analysis was conducted to estimate the %REP using
316	RPE and VL as predictor variables. The validity of the prediction equations was
317	examined through the Pearson’s correlation coeﬃcient (r) with 95% CI via bootstrap-
318	ping; and Bland-Altman plots were used to identify potential systematic bias. The
319	criteria for interpreting the magnitude of the r coeﬃcients were: trivial (0.00–0.09),
320	small (0.10–0.29), moderate (0.30–0.49), large (0.50–0.69), very large (0.70–0.89), nearly
321	perfect (0.90–0.99) and perfect (1.00) (Hopkins, Marshall, Batterham, & Hanin, 2009).
322	Heteroscedasticity of error was deﬁned as an r2 of 0.1 (Atkinson & Nevill, 1998). The
323	level of signiﬁcance was established at p ≤ 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed
324	using the software package SPSS (IBM SPSS version 23.0, Chicago, IL, USA).

404	Discussion and implications
405	This study was designed to analyse the relationships between the RPE, VL and %RPE in
406	the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine following 3 diﬀerent repeti-
407	tion maximum tests. Supporting our ﬁrst hypothesis, the relationships between %REP-
408	RPE and %REP-VL were both very high as revealed by the regression analysis.
409	                                                                 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        51
410	
411	
412	Our second hypothesis was also conﬁrmed since incorporating the RPE together with
413	VL slightly improved the goodness of ﬁt to predict %RPE. Taken together, these
414	ﬁndings highlight that both RPE and VL can be useful variables when attemting to
415	estimate %REP in the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine. Using this
416	approach, strength and conditioning professionals could objectively quantify the level of
417	eﬀort incurred during the bench press exercise performed in a Smith machine.
418	   Previous studies have conﬁrmed the feasibility of RPE for monitoring resistance training
419	due to strong relationships observed between the RPE, relative load (%1RM) and MV
420	(Bautista et al., 2016; Naclerio & Larumbe-Zabala, 2016). However, this study is the ﬁrst to
421	our knowledge that has evaluated the precision of the RPE as a tool for predicting %REP
422	during resistance exercise. Our results show a strong relationship between the RPE and %
423	REP in the bench press exercise. In addition, nearly perfect correlations and trivial
424	systematic bias was observed between actual and predicted %REP values through RPE.
425	Therefore, this study adds evidence that supports the use of RPE scale as a practical tool to
426	objectively quantify the level of eﬀort incurred during resistance training. However, it
427	should be keep in mind that fatigue may be a potencial confounding factor when attemting
428	to utilise RPE in resistance training (Vasquez et al., 2013).
429	   Supporting our ﬁrst hypothesis, a strong relationship was observed between the VL
430	and %RPE, being the goodness of ﬁt comparable to the RPE-%RPE relationship. Similar
431	to the RPE-%REP relationship, nearly perfect correlation and trivial systematic bias
432	were observed between actual and predicted %REP values through VL. The present
433	results agree with those previously presented for the bench press and pull-up exercises
434	(Gonzalez-Badillo et al., 2017; Sanchez-Moreno et al., 2017). Our results revealed
435	a goodness of ﬁt somewhat higher (r2 = 0.91 vs. 0.88 and SEE = 8.96 vs. 9.44%) than
436	those observed during the pull-up exercise (Sanchez-Moreno et al., 2017). However,
437	when comparing our results with those presented for the bench press exercise by
438	Gonzalez-Badillo et al. (2017), a lower r2 (0.91 vs. 0.97) and higher SEE (8.96% vs.
439	5.40%) can be observed. These diﬀerences could be attributed to three methodological
440	diﬀerences: (1) the number of relative intensities used in modelling (3 vs. 8), (2) the
441	analysis procedure of the VL values (pre-established analysis of repetition intervals vs.
442	pre-ﬁxed VL thresholds) and (3) the type of velocity used in the analysis (mean
443	concentric velocity in our study vs. mean concentric propulsive velocity in Gonzalez-
444	Badillo et al. (2017)). Therefore, our results also corroborate that monitoring repetition
445	velocity can be useful approach to provide an accurate estimation of the %RPE during
446	resistance training. Of special note is that the current ﬁndings were obtained during the
447	bench press exercise performed in a Smith machine and, therefore, the ecological
448	validity of measures can be limitated in comparisons with the free-weight bench press
449	exercise. However, it has been previously demonstrated that the incorporation of
450	machine-based testing may provide more reliable velocity measurements when com-
451	pared with free-weight bench exercises (Miller et al., 2018).
452	   To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study that has examined whether
453	incorporating the RPE along with VL as predictor variables in modelling could improve
454	the goodness of ﬁt to predict %REP. Supporting our second hypothesis, the multiple
455	regression analysis shows that utilising both variables (VL and RPE) could increase the
456	explained variance and reduce the SEE compared to the quadratic regressions models
457	using VL or RPE alone. The present results agreed with the study of Balsalobre-Fern
458	 52      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.
459	
460	
461	ández et al. (2018) where the combination of RPE and MV showed higher precision for
462	estimating relative load than the traditional load-velocity relationship. These results
463	indicate that the combination of RPE and VL could be useful for increasing the
464	precision of the eﬀort monitoring process.
465	   The main limitation of the current study was the relatively small sample size, and the
466	fact that the participants presented diﬀerent training backgrounds, which may be
467	a potential confounding factor. Note that previous studies have highlighted that more
468	experienced lifters and those with previous experience using RPE scales could report
469	more accurate estimation of training intensity (i.e., %RM or MV) than novice inexper-
470	ienced lifters (Helms et al., 2017; Zourdos et al., 2016). Futures studies should examine
471	the possible eﬀect of training backgrounds on predication capabilities of the RPE-%REP
472	relationship. It also needs to be considered that the results in our study were obtained
473	during a paused bench-press performed in a Smith machine, and they should not be
474	generalized to other training conditions. Although the load-velocity relationship seems
475	not to dependent on the bench press execution mode (i.e., free-weight or Smith
476	machine) (Loturco et al., 2017), futures studies should examine whether our ﬁndings
477	could be applicable to the free-weight bench press, other free-weight resistance training
478	exercises (e.g., back-squat, deadlift, etc.) as well as other execution techniques (e.g., the
479	eccentric-concentric bench press variant).
480	
481	
482	Conclusions
483	This study conﬁrmed the feasibility of the RPE and VL variables to accurately estimate
484	%REP in each exercise set due to the strong relationships observed between the RPE,
485	VL and %RPE during the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine.
486	However, since the goodness of ﬁt is improved by incorporating RPE or VL as predictor
487	variables, the subjective scale should be considered in conjunction with the velocity
488	measurements to obtain a more precise estimation of the %RPE through the generalised
489	group equation presented in the current study. The results of this study contribute by
490	improving the knowledge regarding the resources that can be used to prescribe,
491	monitor and quantify Smith machine becnch press training . Speciﬁcally, our results
492	are of great practical application because they allow one to objectively quantify the level
493	of eﬀort during each training set in the Smith machine bench press exercise.

Daniel Varela-Olallaa, Juan del Campo-Vecinoa, Marta Leyton-Románb,
Alejandro Pérez-Castilla c and Carlos Balsalobre-Fernández a
a

    ABSTRACT                                                                   ARTICLE HISTORY
    There is a growing interest in the analysis of diﬀerent methods for        Received 7 March 2019
    monitor fatigue during resistance training sessions. This study            Accepted 1 July 2019
    aimed to (1) analyse the relationships between the percentage of           KEYWORDS
    performed repetitions with respect to the maximum possible                 Velocity-based training;
    number (%REP), RPE and magnitude of velocity loss (VL), and (2)            subjective scale; level of
    examine whether a multiple regression analysis with the RPE and            eﬀort; exercise prescription
    VL as predictor variables could improve the goodness of ﬁt to
    predict %REP in the bench press exercise performed in a Smith
    machine. Seven men performed a repetition maximum test, on 3
    separate testing sessions, against 3 diﬀerent absolute loads based
    on a target mean velocity (MV) according to an individual load-
    velocity proﬁle (≈1.00, ≈0.70, and ≈0.50 m/s). MV, VL, %REP and
    RPE were collected and used for analysis. Based upon quadratic
    polynomial regression analysis strong relationships were reported
    between the RPE and %REP (r2 = 0.89 and SEE = 9.85%) and
    between the VL and %REP (r2 = 0.91 and SEE = 9.85%). Multiple
    regression analysis with the RPE and VL as predictor variables
    improved the goodness of ﬁt (r2 = 0.94 and SEE = 7.18%) of the
    model to predict %REP. These results suggest that both RPE and
    VL are useful variables to accurately estimate %REP in the bench
    press exercise.



Introduction
Resistance training has been shown to be a key factor for improving health, body
aesthetics and athletic performance (Balshaw et al., 2017; Folland & Williams, 2007;
Suchomel, Nimphius, & Stone, 2016). However, coaches and sport professionals require
an adequate control of the diﬀerent training variables (e.g., intensity, volume, move-
ment velocity, rest periods, etc.) in order to design an eﬀective resistance training
program (Kraemer & Ratamess, 2004). Among these training variables, the training
intensity and volume seems to be the most important factors impacting the athlete’s
neuromuscular adaptations (Campos et al., 2002; Gonzalez-Badillo, Yanez-Garcia,
Mora-Custodio, & Rodriguez-Rosell, 2017; Munoz-Lopez, Marchante, Cano-Ruiz,
Chicharro, & Balsalobre-Fernandez, 2017).

CONTACT Carlos Balsalobre-Fernández              carlos.balsalobre@uam.es
© 2019 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
 42      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.


    Training intensity has traditionally been based on percentage of the one-repetition
maximum (%1RM) or on the maximum number of repetitions that can be performed
against a submaximal load (Kraemer & Ratamess, 2004; Sakamoto, Sinclair, & Naito,
2016). More recently, is has been suggested that movement velocity may be an appro-
priate way to control training intensity (González-Badillo & Sánchez-Medina, 2010;
Jidovtseﬀ, Harris, Crielaard, & Cronin, 2011; Pareja-Blanco et al., 2017). Previous
studies have observed a strong and stable relationship between movement velocity
and the relative load (%1RM) in a variety of resistance training exercises, mostly
performed in Smith machines (Conceição et al., 2016; García-Ramos, Pestaña-Melero,
Pérez-Castilla, Rojas, & Haﬀ, 2018a; Munoz-Lopez et al., 2017; Pérez-Castilla,
García-Ramos, Padial, Morales-Artacho, & Feriche, 2017). Velocity-based training has
therefore gained popularity in the ﬁeld of strength and conditioning due to the
proliferation of and advancements in sports technology (i.e. linear transducers, accel-
erometers, or mobile applications) that allow for the accurate measurement of move-
ment velocity (Balsalobre-Fernandez et al., 2017; Banyard, Nosaka, Sato, & Haﬀ, 2017;
Pérez-Castilla, Piepoli, Delgado-García, Garrido-Blanca, & García-Ramos, 2019).
However, many of these devices are not able to be practically used within the strength
and conditioning environment and are often not aﬀordable, which limits their ability to
be used by many strength and conditioning professionals (Pérez-Castilla et al., 2019).
    An alternative approach to monitor resistance training intensity based on the
psycho-physiological response of the organism is the ‘rating of perceived exertion’
(RPE) (Day, McGuigan, Brice, & Foster, 2004; Eston & Evans, 2009; Gearhart,
Lagally, Riechman, Andrews, & Robertson, 2009). According to this, the psychologi-
cal/environmental information provokes a subjective perception for a given stimulus
(Borg, 1990). The scales commonly used to collect RPE are the Borg (Borg, 1990) or
OMNI-RES (Robertson et al., 2003) scales. The RPE has been shown to be a useful tool
for predicting the relative load (%1RM) (Day et al., 2004; Eston & Evans, 2009;
Gearhart et al., 2009). However, the relationship between the RPE and resistance
training intensity may be questionated when performing sets to voiluture failure due
to the induced fatigue (Vasquez et al., 2013). Previous investigations have found high
relationship between the RPE, %RM, and MV (Bautista, Chirosa, Robinson, Chirosa, &
Martinez, 2016; Naclerio & Larumbe-Zabala, 2016). Also, a novel scale in which RPE
was based on the number of ‘repetitions in reserve’ (i.e., number of repetitions left in
reserve before reaching muscular failure in a training set; RIR) has been developed
(Zourdos et al., 2016). More importantly, a recent study by Balsalobre-Fernández,
Muñoz-López, Marchante, and García-Ramos (2018) observed that combining RPE,
RIR and movement velocity improves the capabilities of traditional load-velocity
relationships to predict relative loads (%RM). Therefore, it is well documented in
scientiﬁc literature the feasibility of RPE scales to prescribe and monitor training load
according to athlete’s subjective perception.
    Of special note, is that training intensity in isolation is an inadequate predictor of
training adaptation if training volume is not taken into account (Gonzalez-Badillo et al.,
2017). It has been widely argued in the scientiﬁc literature that training to muscular
failure (i.e., performing the maximum number of repetitions possible with a given
relative load) is unnecessary for maximising athletic performance (Davies, Orr, Halaki,
& Hackett, 2016; Izquierdo et al., 2006). Velocity loss (VL) has been recently proposed
                                                                 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        43


as a precise and non-invasive variable to monitor the actual degree or level of eﬀort
incurred during resistance training (Sánchez-Medina & González-Badillo, 2011).
Previous studies have reported a strong relationship between the relative VL in
a training set and the percentage of performed repetitions with respect to the maximum
possible number that can be completed (%REP) in the bench press and pull-up
exercises in a smith machine (Gonzalez-Badillo et al., 2017; Sanchez-Moreno,
Rodriguez-Rosell, Pareja-Blanco, Mora-Custodio, & Gonzalez-Badillo, 2017). By mon-
itoring repetition velocity can be accurately estimated with the %RPE (or RIR) when
a given percentage of VL is achieved during a training set. However, no known studies
have analysed whether the subjective RPE scale is able to estimate the %RPE with
similar precision to that seen with the VL method. It also remains unknown whether
incorporating the RPE along with VL has additional predication capabilities to mon-
itoring %RPE.
   In line with the aforementioned considerations, the objectives of the present study
were to (1) analyse the relationships between the %REP, RPE and VL, and (2) examine
whether a multiple regression analysis with the RPE and VL as predictor variables could
improve the precision of the prediction of the %REP in the bench press exercise
performed in a Smith machine. We hypothesised that (1) no diﬀerence would be
observed between the RPE and VL in the precision of the prediction of %REP, (2)
a more precise estimation of the %RPE would be obtained using RPE and VL as
predictor variables.


Methods
Participants
The sample size was determined based on previous studies (Sreckovic et al., 2015;
Zivkovic, Djuric, Cuk, Suzovic, & Jaric, 2017), which calculated that a sample size
between 3 and 12 participants was needed to detect diﬀerences on mechanical para-
meters observed from the loaded bench press executions with a signiﬁcant level of
p < 0.005 and desired statistical at 0.8. Therefore, we recruited 7 physically active men
(age: 22.9 ± 1.9 years; body mass: 77.8 ± 11.7 kg; height: 1.76 ± 0.68 m) volunteered to
participate in this study. Participants had at least 1 year of resistance training experience
and a bench press 1RM of 83.6 ± 16.4 kg (1.08 ± 0.20 kg/kg body mass). No physical
limitations, health problems or musculoskeletal injuries that could compromise tested
performance were reported. None of the participants were taking drugs, medications or
other substances that could alter their physical performance. Participants were
informed of the study procedures and signed a written informed consent form prior
to initiating the study. The study protocol adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of
Helsinki and was approved by the Institutional Review Board at the University of
Granada.


Experimental design
A cross-sectional study was designed to examine the RPE-%REP-VL relationships in
the bench press exercise. Participant undertook 3 testing session, at the same time of
 44      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.


the day for each participant, separated by 72–96 hours of rest between them. In each
testing session, participants completed a repetition maximum test against an external
load based on a target mean velocity (MV) according to previously established indivi-
dual load-velocity proﬁle (≈1.00, ≈0.70, and ≈0.50 m/s). The individual load-velocity
relationship was was determined based upon the completion of a standardized incre-
mental load testing until a 1RM has been achieved (García-Ramos et al., 2018a). During
the repeptition maximum test, the RPE scale was inmediately shown to the participants
and they were asked to verbally rating the RPE value during each analysis interval
previously established (see above for further details). The main variables analysed were:
1) mean velocity (MV) of each repetition; 2) MV of the fastest repetition (MVBEST)
during the repetition maximum test; 3) MV of the last repetition (MVLAST) during the
repetition maximum test; 4) velocity loss (VL) over each analysis interval calculated as
100*(MVBEST—MV/MVBEST); 5) percentage of repetitions completed (%REP) with
respect to the maximum possible number over each analysis interval; and 6) rating of
perceived exertion (RPE) verbally reported over each analysis interval.


Testing procedures
Familiarisation and initial measures
In the 2 weeks prior to the study, participants performed 2 familiarisation sessions,
separated by 7 days, to ensure a proper technique during the bench press exercise and
familiarise participants with Borg’s RPE (1–10) scale (Borg, 1990). In the ﬁrst familiar-
isation session, the anthropometric measures (height and body mass) were taken and
then participants carried out a standard incremental loading test to determine the
individual load-velocity proﬁle (García-Ramos, Pestaña-Melero, Pérez-Castilla, Rojas,
& Haﬀ, 2018b). In the second familiarisation session, participants performed several
warm-up sets of 3–8 repetitions with diﬀerent external loads and, subsequently, had to
verbally report the RPE value after each set. Thereafter, they carried out a repetition
maximum test against an external load based on a target MV of ≈0.70 m/s according to
the previously established individual load-velocity proﬁle in order to experience
a maximum eﬀort (i.e., RPE 10).

Load-velocity proﬁle determination
Before the commencement of the load-velocity test, participants performed
a standardised warm-up consisting of 5 min of joint mobility, followed by 2 sets of
10 and 8 repetitions (interspaced with 2 min rest) with an external load of 20 and 30 kg
respectively. After warming up, the individual load-velocity relationship was deter-
mined by means of a standard incremental loading test performed in a Smith machine
(Technogym, Barcelona, Spain) (García-Ramos et al., 2018a). The initial external load
of the incremental loading test was set at 20 kg. Thereafter, the load was progressively
increased in 10 kg increments until the MV was lower than 0.50 m/s. From that
moment, the load was progressively increased in steps of 5 to 2.5 kg until the 1RM
strength was achieved. For the lighter loads (MV ≥ 0.80 m/s), 3 repetitions were
performed at each load, 2 for medium loads (0.80 m/s > MV ≥ 0.5 m/s), and only 1
for the heavier loads (MV < 0.5 m/s). Participants were verbally asked to provide a RPE
value after each load lifted in order to familiarise them with this RPE scale.
                                                               SPORTS BIOMECHANICS       45


   The bench press technique involved the participants laying supine on ﬂat bench,
with their feet fully supported on the ﬂoor and their hands placed on the bar with a self-
selected grip-width, which was slightly wider than shoulder width. The self-selected grip
width was individually measured and kept constant throughout all testing sessions. The
position on the bench was individually adjusted with the vertical projection of the bar
corresponding with the participant’s mid line of the chest. Participants were required to
lower the bar in a controlled manner until contacting their chest. After maintaining
a momentary pause for ≈1–1.5 s, they performed a purely concentric action at the
maximum possible velocity. The momentary pause between phases was imposed in
order to minimise the eﬀect of the stretch-shortening cycle and the contribution of
elastic energy to the movement as proposed previously (Pareja-Blanco et al., 2017).

Repetition maximum test
Participants completed a standardised warm-up consisted of 5 min of joint mobility,
followed by 4 sets of 10 repetitions against 20 kg, 5 repetitions against 30 kg, 5
repetitions against 40 kg and 2 repetitions against 50 kg (interspaced with 2 min
rest). If the participant reported a higher 1RM than 80 kg, an additional set of 2
repetitions against 60 kg was completed. Afterward, participants performed
a repetition maximum test based on completing the maximum number of possible
repetitions with a submaximal load previously determined according to the individual
load-velocity proﬁle. Speciﬁcally, the absolute loads (kg) were established based on
a target MV reached at the ﬁrst 1–3 repetitions (usually the fastest) during each
repetition maximum test: load 1 = ≈1.00 m/s, load 2 = ≈0.70 m/s, and load
3 = ≈0.50 m/s. The repetition maximum test ended when participants were unable to
perform a repetition with a proper technique or when a completed range of motion was
not reached (Pérez-Castilla, Suzovic, Domanovic, Fernandes, & García-Ramos, 2019).
A pause of 2 s. was imposed between the eccentric and concentric phases of each
repetition. During each repetition maximum test, the RPE value was inmediately
requested from the participant in pre-established analysis intervals: every 5, 3 and 2
repetitions during the load 1 (≈1.00 m/s), 2 (≈0.70 m/s), and 3 (≈0.50 m/s), respectively.

Measurement equipment and data analysis
Anthropometric variables (height and body mass) were measured with a digital stadi-
ometer with scale (SECA 220, SECA, Germany). A Smith machine (Technogym,
Barcelona, Spain) was used for all tests. An isoinertial dynamometer (ChronojumpTH
Boscosystem, Barcelona, Spain), which consists of a cable-extension linear position
transducer attached to the bar interfaced with a personal computer at a sampling rate
of 1,000 Hz, was used for mechanical measurements. Speciﬁcally MV, which is deter-
mined by the diﬀerentiation of the displacement data with respect to time, was auto-
matically calculated by the custom software v.1.8.1–54. Reliability and validity of this
device has been previously reported else where (Pérez-Castilla et al., 2019). A visual
presentation of Borg’s RPE scale (1–10) was used throughout testing.

Statistical analyses
Descriptive data are presented as means, standard deviations (SD) and coeﬃcients of
variation (CV) with the corresponding 95% conﬁdence intervals (CI). The distribution
 46      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.


of the variables was analysed by the Kolmogorov-Smirnov tests. The non-parametric
Kruskal-Wallis H tests were used to compare dependent variables between the repeti-
tion maximum tests. Mann-Whitney U tests were used to identify the source of any
signiﬁcant diﬀerence. Quadratic polynomial regression models were used to examine
the relationship between %REP, RPE and VL. The goodness of ﬁt was assessed by the
Pearson’s multivariate coeﬃcient of determination (r2) and the standard error of the
estimate (SEE). Multiple regression analysis was conducted to estimate the %REP using
RPE and VL as predictor variables. The validity of the prediction equations was
examined through the Pearson’s correlation coeﬃcient (r) with 95% CI via bootstrap-
ping; and Bland-Altman plots were used to identify potential systematic bias. The
criteria for interpreting the magnitude of the r coeﬃcients were: trivial (0.00–0.09),
small (0.10–0.29), moderate (0.30–0.49), large (0.50–0.69), very large (0.70–0.89), nearly
perfect (0.90–0.99) and perfect (1.00) (Hopkins, Marshall, Batterham, & Hanin, 2009).
Heteroscedasticity of error was deﬁned as an r2 of 0.1 (Atkinson & Nevill, 1998). The
level of signiﬁcance was established at p ≤ 0.05. Statistical analyses were performed
using the software package SPSS (IBM SPSS version 23.0, Chicago, IL, USA).


Results
Descriptive data
The Kruskal-Wallis H test only revealed signiﬁcant diﬀerences for the variables VL
(Chi2: 7.85) and repetitions (Chi2: 17.4). The pairwise comparisons are reported in
Table 1.


%REP-RPE and %REP-VL relationships
Quadratic polynomial regressions for the relationship between the RPE-%REP and
between the VL-%REP are presented in Figure 1. Multiple regression analysis for
the prediction of %REP (dependent variable) by RPE and VL (independent vari-
ables) obtained from the whole dataset (n = 140) reported a high goodness of ﬁt
(r2 = 0.94; SEE = 7.18%; p < 0.001) following the next equation: %REP = 0.76VL +
4.27RPE—2.07.


Validity of the equations to predict %REP
When analysing the whole dataset (n = 140), nearly perfect correlations (r range = 0.94–
0.95; SEE range = 8.52–9.24%) between the actual and predicted %REP values were
observed for both the RPE and VL relationship (Figure 2). Similarly, the Bland-Altman
plots showed trivial systematic bias (%REP predicted by RPE = −0.00%; %REP pre-
dicted by VL = −0.05%) and moderate random errors (%REP predicted by
RPE = 9.78%; %REP predicted by VL = 8.89%) (Figure 3). No heteroscedasticity of
the errors was observed (r2 range = 0.02–0.03).

Discussion and implications
This study was designed to analyse the relationships between the RPE, VL and %RPE in
the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine following 3 diﬀerent repeti-
tion maximum tests. Supporting our ﬁrst hypothesis, the relationships between %REP-
RPE and %REP-VL were both very high as revealed by the regression analysis.
                                                                 SPORTS BIOMECHANICS        51


Our second hypothesis was also conﬁrmed since incorporating the RPE together with
VL slightly improved the goodness of ﬁt to predict %RPE. Taken together, these
ﬁndings highlight that both RPE and VL can be useful variables when attemting to
estimate %REP in the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine. Using this
approach, strength and conditioning professionals could objectively quantify the level of
eﬀort incurred during the bench press exercise performed in a Smith machine.
   Previous studies have conﬁrmed the feasibility of RPE for monitoring resistance training
due to strong relationships observed between the RPE, relative load (%1RM) and MV
(Bautista et al., 2016; Naclerio & Larumbe-Zabala, 2016). However, this study is the ﬁrst to
our knowledge that has evaluated the precision of the RPE as a tool for predicting %REP
during resistance exercise. Our results show a strong relationship between the RPE and %
REP in the bench press exercise. In addition, nearly perfect correlations and trivial
systematic bias was observed between actual and predicted %REP values through RPE.
Therefore, this study adds evidence that supports the use of RPE scale as a practical tool to
objectively quantify the level of eﬀort incurred during resistance training. However, it
should be keep in mind that fatigue may be a potencial confounding factor when attemting
to utilise RPE in resistance training (Vasquez et al., 2013).
   Supporting our ﬁrst hypothesis, a strong relationship was observed between the VL
and %RPE, being the goodness of ﬁt comparable to the RPE-%RPE relationship. Similar
to the RPE-%REP relationship, nearly perfect correlation and trivial systematic bias
were observed between actual and predicted %REP values through VL. The present
results agree with those previously presented for the bench press and pull-up exercises
(Gonzalez-Badillo et al., 2017; Sanchez-Moreno et al., 2017). Our results revealed
a goodness of ﬁt somewhat higher (r2 = 0.91 vs. 0.88 and SEE = 8.96 vs. 9.44%) than
those observed during the pull-up exercise (Sanchez-Moreno et al., 2017). However,
when comparing our results with those presented for the bench press exercise by
Gonzalez-Badillo et al. (2017), a lower r2 (0.91 vs. 0.97) and higher SEE (8.96% vs.
5.40%) can be observed. These diﬀerences could be attributed to three methodological
diﬀerences: (1) the number of relative intensities used in modelling (3 vs. 8), (2) the
analysis procedure of the VL values (pre-established analysis of repetition intervals vs.
pre-ﬁxed VL thresholds) and (3) the type of velocity used in the analysis (mean
concentric velocity in our study vs. mean concentric propulsive velocity in Gonzalez-
Badillo et al. (2017)). Therefore, our results also corroborate that monitoring repetition
velocity can be useful approach to provide an accurate estimation of the %RPE during
resistance training. Of special note is that the current ﬁndings were obtained during the
bench press exercise performed in a Smith machine and, therefore, the ecological
validity of measures can be limitated in comparisons with the free-weight bench press
exercise. However, it has been previously demonstrated that the incorporation of
machine-based testing may provide more reliable velocity measurements when com-
pared with free-weight bench exercises (Miller et al., 2018).
   To the best of our knowledge, this is the ﬁrst study that has examined whether
incorporating the RPE along with VL as predictor variables in modelling could improve
the goodness of ﬁt to predict %REP. Supporting our second hypothesis, the multiple
regression analysis shows that utilising both variables (VL and RPE) could increase the
explained variance and reduce the SEE compared to the quadratic regressions models
using VL or RPE alone. The present results agreed with the study of Balsalobre-Fern
 52      D. VARELA-OLALLA ET AL.


ández et al. (2018) where the combination of RPE and MV showed higher precision for
estimating relative load than the traditional load-velocity relationship. These results
indicate that the combination of RPE and VL could be useful for increasing the
precision of the eﬀort monitoring process.
   The main limitation of the current study was the relatively small sample size, and the
fact that the participants presented diﬀerent training backgrounds, which may be
a potential confounding factor. Note that previous studies have highlighted that more
experienced lifters and those with previous experience using RPE scales could report
more accurate estimation of training intensity (i.e., %RM or MV) than novice inexper-
ienced lifters (Helms et al., 2017; Zourdos et al., 2016). Futures studies should examine
the possible eﬀect of training backgrounds on predication capabilities of the RPE-%REP
relationship. It also needs to be considered that the results in our study were obtained
during a paused bench-press performed in a Smith machine, and they should not be
generalized to other training conditions. Although the load-velocity relationship seems
not to dependent on the bench press execution mode (i.e., free-weight or Smith
machine) (Loturco et al., 2017), futures studies should examine whether our ﬁndings
could be applicable to the free-weight bench press, other free-weight resistance training
exercises (e.g., back-squat, deadlift, etc.) as well as other execution techniques (e.g., the
eccentric-concentric bench press variant).


Conclusions
This study conﬁrmed the feasibility of the RPE and VL variables to accurately estimate
%REP in each exercise set due to the strong relationships observed between the RPE,
VL and %RPE during the bench press exercise performed with a Smith machine.
However, since the goodness of ﬁt is improved by incorporating RPE or VL as predictor
variables, the subjective scale should be considered in conjunction with the velocity
measurements to obtain a more precise estimation of the %RPE through the generalised
group equation presented in the current study. The results of this study contribute by
improving the knowledge regarding the resources that can be used to prescribe,
monitor and quantify Smith machine becnch press training . Speciﬁcally, our results
are of great practical application because they allow one to objectively quantify the level
of eﬀort during each training set in the Smith machine bench press exercise.

We would like to thank all the participants who selﬂessly participated in the study.

No potential conﬂict of interest was reported by the authors.

56

58	a

66	    practitioners and is widely used in the prescription and monitoring                        Accepted 9 March 2021
67	    of physical conditioning programmes. Although a number of meth­                            KEYWORDS
68	    ods of load quantification are used, a common feature is that total                        word; training load; TRIMP;
69	    load calculations are the product of exercise intensity and duration.                      RPE
70	    We argue that these methods may be limited, however, as they do
71	    not account for non-linearities in the biological response to stress,
72	    with the end result being that they fail to fully account for the load
73	    imposed by high-intensity or interval-based training sessions. We
74	    end with a call for sport scientists to develop novel method of
75	    training load quantification to better deal with this issue.
76	
77

79	Introduction
80	There is understandably great interest in the monitoring of athlete training loads. It is not
81	the purpose of this brief commentary to explore in detail the various methods used in this
82	process, but, in general, we refer to load as the net stimulus or “dose” of a training session,
83	which is typically quantified as a single unit combining exercise intensity and volume (i.e.,
84	duration)(Impellizzeri et al., 2019). This can be thought of as an impulse-type metric; that
85	is, not in a mechanical sense (nor is the term “load”), but as an analogy to describe the area
86	under the curve represented by duration (x-axis) and exercise intensity (y-axis). The
87	resulting “score” can be used to track training load over time and manage the training
88	process. Two of the most common load metrics are session ratings of perceived exertion
89	(sRPE., i.e., sRPE-TL) (Foster, 1998) and heart-rate-derived training impulse (TRIMP)
90	(Bannister, 1991; Edwards, 1993).
91	    Whilst recognizing the value of these methods, we propose to use this commentary to
92	highlight a potential shortcoming that is seldom discussed. Nassim Taleb (2012) uses the
93	term “Antifragile” to describe objects or systems that respond to stress not by breaking (as
94	would a fragile object or system), but by adapting and becoming stronger. This is exactly
95	the process an athlete takes advantage of, through a hormetic response whereby specific
96	functional adaptations result in improved performance capacity. Taleb tells the story of
97	the ancient king who, in a rage, decreed that his son must be punished for some misdeed
98	
99	CONTACT Andrew Renfree              a.renfree@worc.ac.uk       School of Sport & Exercise Science, University of Worcester,
100	Worcester, UK
101	© 2021 Informa UK Limited, trading as Taylor & Francis Group
102	 2      A. RENFREE ET AL.
103	
104	
105	and that the punishment would consist of having a boulder dropped on his head from
106	a great height, an almost certainly fatal event. As the day of the punishment grew closer,
107	the king started to regret his decision, but also did not want to be seen as “weak” by his
108	subjects. However, his advisors developed an elegant solution to the king’s dilemma –
109	instead of dropping the boulder all in one go, it was broken into 1000 small pebbles which
110	were dropped one by one. Through this method, the same total load was “applied” to the
111	son but instead of a fatal outcome, the end result was mild discomfort. This story
112	illustrates a key feature of the biological response to stress, that of non-linearity. Whilst
113	the total load remained the same, the stress response depended on the way in which it
114	was applied. Applying it all at once had a greater impact than spreading the load out over
115	a longer period.
116	
117	
118	Discussion
119	We suggest the same principles hold true for physical training – that the manner in which
120	a load is applied is equally or more important than the magnitude of the load. As
121	a hypothetical example, a 30-minute bout of exercise at an sRPE of 5 arbitrary units (au)
122	and a 15-minute maximal bout at an sRPE of 10 au both generate an sRPE-TL of 150 au.
123	Similarly, two sessions consisting of 20 minutes at 80–90% maximum heart rate or
124	40 minutes at 60–70% maximum heart rate would each render an Edwards TRIMP of 80
125	au. However, using the argument outlined above, the shorter session imposes greater
126	physiological stress. To further illustrate this problem, consider a typical pre-competition
127	phase session for a middle-distance runner consisting of 2 × 400 m at maximal effort, with
128	full recovery between repetitions. Although sRPE may be maximal, the short duration of
129	the session (approximately 0.8 minutes per repetition) means the total load imposed by
130	the repetitions is very small (16 au). This also means a very easy warm-down jog at the end
131	of the session may produce a greater TRIMP than the main activity in what is a very
132	difficult training session likely to produce a high signal for adaptation.
133	    A similar issue exists when small-sided games are utilized as a conditioning modality
134	for team sport athletes, in that use of overall sRPE or TRIMP fail to take into account the
135	intermittent nature of the activity. We consider this of crucial importance as the result may
136	be significant underestimation of the load imposed by high-intensity sessions relative to
137	low-intensity sessions. This point is illustrated in Figure 1, using hypothetical training
138	periods for endurance and team sports. Regardless of the method used, some days render
139	identical training load scores (data labels) despite vastly differing combinations of inten­
140	sity and volume.
141	    The issue of interval training is further complicated by the requirement to consider the
142	influence of recovery time between high-intensity bouts. Manipulation of session density
143	through changes in the duration of recovery periods can influence total session duration.
144	If, in order to account for total exercise duration, activity during recovery periods are
145	included in total load calculations, we can envisage a situation whereby increasing
146	duration of recovery actually increases calculated session load, even if the physiological
147	stress imposed is lower. Additionally, the mode of activity between bouts of high-intensity
148	exercise must be considered. An active recovery may impose lower metabolic stress than
149	passive recovery between repetitions of sprint interval training (Wahl & Mathes, 2020),
150	despite a higher average heart rate during recovery periods. Here then, we have another

160	situation whereby a training load calculation using TRIMP results in a higher loading score
161	for a session that may be expected to produce less physiological stress.
162	   Advancements in training load quantification over the past two decades have seen the
163	advent of several different methods to improve its precision: the use of category-ratio
164	scaling – and in particular the CR100® (centiMax) scale (Borg & Borg, 2001) – to account for
165	the non-linear exercise–response relationship when measuring sRPE and individualized
166	TRIMP (Manzi et al., 2009), which includes an exponential weighting coefficient based on
167	an athlete’s maximally graded HR–blood-lactate association. However, despite these
168	sophistications, there will always exist a situation whereby two sessions consisting of
169	vastly differing combinations of intensity and volume will render almost identical load
170	values (Figure 1). Furthermore, we acknowledge that while the examples we provide
171	focus on single load measures, a multitude of data sources are clearly needed for effective
172	decision-making. Nevertheless, we maintain that the fundamental issues we identify will
173	persist, a point recently made by Gamble et al. (2020) who emphasize practitioners should
174	be “data-informed” rather than “data-driven”. Unfortunately, it is not within the scope of
175	this brief commentary to speculate in regard to solutions to this issue. However, we feel it

183	training decisions. To exemplify this, we refer to Figure 1 as a seemingly straightforward
184	but powerful visualization strategy that could help coaches and practitioners better
185	understand the nature of (internal) training load.

20	Abstract
21	This study investigated the return to baseline of movement velocity and maximal strength following a strength-
22	orientated session and power-orientated session in the free-weight back-squat performed with maximal concentric
23	velocity. Fourteen strength-trained males completed a strength-orientated session (five sets of five repetitions @80% of
24	a one-repetition maximum) and a power-orientated session (three sets of six repetitions @50% one-repetition max-
25	imum ) in a randomised order over two weeks (e.g. strength week 1, power week 2). The back-squat was then
26	performed with loads of 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 90% and 100% one-repetition maximum at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h following
27	the strength and power exercise sessions to assess return to baseline of squat velocity and maximal strength. Dependent
28	variables included one-repetition maximum, back-squat mean velocity and peak velocity and countermovement jump
29	peak velocity. Meaningful changes ((effect size)  0.60) were reported for mean velocity and peak velocity at
30	loads  60% one-repetition maximum at 24 and 48 h after the strength-orientated session. Trivial to small (effect
31	size  0.59) differences were reported for squat velocities following the power-orientated session. Only trivial to
32	small effect size differences were observed for countermovement jump peak velocity and one-repetition maximum at all
33	time points following both sessions. Squat velocity (mean velocity and peak velocity) across the load–velocity profile had
34	recovered at 72 h following the strength-orientated session. However, the return to baseline of squat velocity (mean
35	velocity and peak velocity) did not coincide with the return to baseline of one-repetition maximum or countermove-
36	ment jump peak velocity. Therefore, measuring and monitoring meaningful changes in velocity may be a more valid and
37	practical alternative in determining full recovery and readiness to train.

Abstract
This study investigated the return to baseline of movement velocity and maximal strength following a strength-
orientated session and power-orientated session in the free-weight back-squat performed with maximal concentric
velocity. Fourteen strength-trained males completed a strength-orientated session (five sets of five repetitions @80% of
a one-repetition maximum) and a power-orientated session (three sets of six repetitions @50% one-repetition max-
imum ) in a randomised order over two weeks (e.g. strength week 1, power week 2). The back-squat was then
performed with loads of 20%, 40%, 60%, 80%, 90% and 100% one-repetition maximum at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h following
the strength and power exercise sessions to assess return to baseline of squat velocity and maximal strength. Dependent
variables included one-repetition maximum, back-squat mean velocity and peak velocity and countermovement jump
peak velocity. Meaningful changes ((effect size)  0.60) were reported for mean velocity and peak velocity at
loads  60% one-repetition maximum at 24 and 48 h after the strength-orientated session. Trivial to small (effect
size  0.59) differences were reported for squat velocities following the power-orientated session. Only trivial to
small effect size differences were observed for countermovement jump peak velocity and one-repetition maximum at all
time points following both sessions. Squat velocity (mean velocity and peak velocity) across the load–velocity profile had
recovered at 72 h following the strength-orientated session. However, the return to baseline of squat velocity (mean
velocity and peak velocity) did not coincide with the return to baseline of one-repetition maximum or countermove-
ment jump peak velocity. Therefore, measuring and monitoring meaningful changes in velocity may be a more valid and
practical alternative in determining full recovery and readiness to train.

Keywords
Back squat, countermovement jump, load-velocity profile, one-repetition maximum, resistance training

  "abstract": "The study tracked the return to baseline of back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity over 96 h after a strength-oriented session and a power-oriented session in strength-trained men. The authors conclude that velocity monitoring may be a more practical guide to full recovery and readiness to train than 1RM or jump testing.",
  "tldr": "After a heavy back-squat session, bar speed at 60% 1RM and above stayed below baseline until 48 h and was back to baseline by 72 h, while 1RM and jump peak velocity recovered within 24 h. Velocity may be a more sensitive readiness check than 1RM or a jump test, though this rests on one protocol in 14 to 15 men.",
  "methods": "Repeated-measures crossover study in which strength-trained men completed a strength session (five sets of five at 80% 1RM) and a power session (six sets of three at 50% 1RM) in random order, one week apart. After a baseline 1RM and load-velocity profile, back-squat mean and peak velocity, 1RM and countermovement jump peak velocity were measured at 24, 48, 72 and 96 h using a linear position transducer. Cohen's d of 0.60 or more was treated as a meaningful change from baseline.",
  "findings": "After the strength session, mean and peak velocity were moderately reduced at 60%, 80% and 90% 1RM at 24 and 48 h, with no meaningful change at 72 or 96 h. Velocity at 20% and 40% 1RM showed no meaningful decrease. Maximal strength and countermovement jump peak velocity showed only trivial to small changes at all times after either session, and the power session produced only trivial to small velocity changes.",
  "limitations": "The sample is small, all male, and studied with one back-squat protocol, so findings do not apply to other lifts or to athletes without this training history. The authors state the countermovement jump may not be sensitive enough to detect strength-session fatigue. The abstract describes the power session as three sets of six and the Methods as six sets of three, and gives 14 completers against 15 recruited; the Methods values are reported here.",
  "practicalImplications": "After a heavy strength session, a coach could delay heavy (60% 1RM and above) velocity-based work until about 72 h, and check bar speed at fixed loads before loading rather than relying on 1RM or jump tests. The study does not show that velocity checks improve later training results.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Bar speed at 60% 1RM and above recovered by 72 h after a heavy back-squat session, so coaches could use a fixed-load velocity check to decide when to repeat heavy lower-body work. The study did not test whether timing heavy work this way improves later strength gains.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The men had no current musculoskeletal injury and the study did not include injured athletes, so it cannot inform return to sport. It cannot show that velocity recovery signals readiness after injury."

}

  "citation": "Jones B, Tooby J, Weaving D, Till K, Owen C, Begonia M, et al. Ready for impact? A validity and feasibility study of instrumented mouthguards (iMGs). Br J Sports Med. 2022.",
  "doi": "10.1136/bjsports-2022-105523",
  "abstract": "This four-phase study assessed the laboratory validity, on-field validity, player feasibility and practitioner feasibility of four instrumented mouthguard systems in rugby league. Laboratory kinematics were compared with a headform reference, on-field events were checked against video, 18 players rated fit, comfort and function, and four practitioners rated usability. Total concordance was high for three systems and low for ORB, on-field performance differed between systems, and player and practitioner ratings favoured HitIQ and Prevent.",
  "tldr": "The four mouthguard systems differed widely: Biocore-FRI, HitIQ and Prevent matched the laboratory headform closely, and Prevent gave the best combined on-field performance. Teams should check mouthguard events against video before using the counts for player welfare or research.",
  "methods": "Four-phase study. Phase I compared peak linear and angular kinematics from each system with a headform reference at 25 to 100 g. Phase II compared triggered events in 80 player-match observations (51 male players, nine matches) with video verification to calculate positive predictive value and sensitivity. Phase III had 18 players rate fit, comfort and function after two training sessions, and Phase IV had four practitioners complete the System Usability Scale.",
  "findings": "Total concordance correlation coefficients were 0.986 (Biocore-FRI), 0.965 (HitIQ), 0.525 (ORB) and 0.984 (Prevent). Positive predictive values were 0.98, 0.90, 0.53 and 0.94, and sensitivity was 0.51, 0.40, 0.71 and 0.75. Counting off-camera and inactive assumed false positives lowered positive predictive values to 0.81, 0.60, 0.37 and 0.89. Player fit was highest for HitIQ (88%) and Prevent (85%), and practitioner usability scores were 83.8 and 80.0 for Prevent and 71.3 and 78.8 for HitIQ (preparation and management), against 51.3 and 50.6 for Biocore-FRI.",
  "limitations": "Only one camera view followed the ball, so some events could not be verified and were classed as assumed false positives. Recording thresholds were set by each company and affected sensitivity, and the on-field kinematics were not validated. The authors note that the study may have favoured systems previously tested in the laboratory or used in rugby league, and several authors have ties to Prevent Biometrics.",
  "practicalImplications": "When choosing an instrumented mouthguard, staff should weigh false positives and false negatives together rather than one alone, and check on-field events against video before using counts for welfare or research decisions. Kinematic values differ between systems, so peak values from one system should not be compared directly with another's.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Head acceleration counts from these mouthguards depend heavily on the system used, so a monitoring team should pick one system, check its events against video, and avoid comparing counts across brands. The study does not link the data to any performance outcome.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study did not link mouthguard data to concussion diagnosis or return-to-play decisions. The authors state that kinematic data in isolation may not support clinical decisions, so this study cannot show that these devices can guide return to play."
 }
}

  "doi": "10.1055/a-2270-3306",
  "abstract": "The study surveyed athletes about 2 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction to find whether they had returned to their pre-injury sport level and, if not, why, and which factors were linked to the main reasons. Only 10% of the 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury level. Lack of confidence or fear of re-injury and post-surgical knee impairment were the most common reasons, and knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment.",
  "tldr": "Only 10% of 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury sport level two years after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction. Fear of re-injury, low confidence and knee impairment were the main reasons given, and giving-way episodes were the only factor tied to ongoing knee impairment.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional survey of athletes aged 14 to 50 who had a primary hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction 1 to 5 years earlier and played level I or II sports, carried out between July 2017 and August 2018. Athletes completed a self-administered questionnaire on pre-injury sport, return to sport, knee giving-way and second knee injuries, and chose and ranked reasons for not returning, with injuries confirmed by MRI and surgical reports. Univariate logistic regression tested predictors of the two most common reasons.",
  "findings": "Nine of 91 athletes (10%; 95% CI 4.6 to 17.9%) had returned to their pre-injury level at a mean follow-up of 1.8 years. Among the 82 who gave reasons, lack of confidence or fear of re-injury was most common (56 athletes, 68.3%), followed by post-surgical knee impairment (43 athletes, 52.4%), and little time or work and family obligations (each 23.2%). Knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment as a reason (OR 8.3, 95% CI 2.48 to 27.42, p = 0.001), and no variable significantly predicted fear or lack of confidence.",
  "limitations": "The cross-sectional, self-report design carries recall bias, and about 30% of eligible athletes did not respond or were lost, although the authors found no demographic differences. Only two women took part, so results cannot be generalised to women, and rehabilitation was not standardised. Knee giving-way was not confirmed by clinical tests or MRI, and the sample is small.",
  "practicalImplications": "Rehabilitation should check fear, confidence and knee impairment, for example by assessing psychological status, explaining expected timelines and gradually exposing athletes to higher knee demands. Athletes who report giving-way should have dynamic knee stability addressed before high-demand sport, and their own view of knee impairment should be asked about during rehabilitation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Reported giving-way was tied to ongoing knee impairment, so performance staff should watch for it during return-to-training and build dynamic knee stability work before high-demand sessions. Fear and low confidence were the leading reasons athletes had not returned, and the authors suggest addressing them with psychological checks and graded exposure.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The study explains why athletes 1 to 5 years after reconstruction had not returned, so it can guide which psychological and knee-stability items to check before clearance. It did not identify criteria that predict return, and it cannot show that addressing these reasons raises return rates."

 "paper": {
  "year": 2024,

  "doi": "10.1055/a-2270-3306",
  "abstract": "The study surveyed athletes about 2 years after hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction to find whether they had returned to their pre-injury sport level and, if not, why, and which factors were linked to the main reasons. Only 10% of the 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury level. Lack of confidence or fear of re-injury and post-surgical knee impairment were the most common reasons, and knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment.",
  "tldr": "Only 10% of 91 athletes had returned to their pre-injury sport level two years after hamstring-graft ACL reconstruction. Fear of re-injury, low confidence and knee impairment were the main reasons given, and giving-way episodes were the only factor tied to ongoing knee impairment.",
  "methods": "Cross-sectional survey of athletes aged 14 to 50 who had a primary hamstring-autograft ACL reconstruction 1 to 5 years earlier and played level I or II sports, carried out between July 2017 and August 2018. Athletes completed a self-administered questionnaire on pre-injury sport, return to sport, knee giving-way and second knee injuries, and chose and ranked reasons for not returning, with injuries confirmed by MRI and surgical reports. Univariate logistic regression tested predictors of the two most common reasons.",
  "findings": "Nine of 91 athletes (10%; 95% CI 4.6 to 17.9%) had returned to their pre-injury level at a mean follow-up of 1.8 years. Among the 82 who gave reasons, lack of confidence or fear of re-injury was most common (56 athletes, 68.3%), followed by post-surgical knee impairment (43 athletes, 52.4%), and little time or work and family obligations (each 23.2%). Knee giving-way was the only significant predictor of knee impairment as a reason (OR 8.3, 95% CI 2.48 to 27.42, p = 0.001), and no variable significantly predicted fear or lack of confidence.",
  "limitations": "The cross-sectional, self-report design carries recall bias, and about 30% of eligible athletes did not respond or were lost, although the authors found no demographic differences.   "practicalImplications": "Rehabilitation should check fear, confidence and knee impairment, for example by assessing psychological status, explaining expected timelines and gradually exposing athletes to higher knee demands. Athletes who report giving-way should have dynamic knee stability addressed before high-demand sport, and their own view of knee impairment should be asked about during rehabilitation.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Reported giving-way was tied to ongoing knee impairment, so performance staff should watch for it during return-to-training and build dynamic knee stability work before high-demand sessions. 13	  Abstract
14	  Objective: Prescription opioid misuse has become a significant public health issue. Previous research has examined predictors of
15	  prescription opioid use and misuse among former National Football League (NFL) players. The present study aimed to describe how
16	  reasons for prescription opioid use while in the NFL corresponds to use and misuse in retirement. Design: Former NFL players
17	  reporting prescription opioid use during their playing careers (N 5 336) were included in this secondary data analysis. Participants
18	  reported reasons for prescription opioid use, including pain management, use “to function,” to improve mood, to reduce stress, and
19	  to aid sleep. Results: Among retired NFL players with exposure to prescribed pain medication during their playing career, 26.2%
20	  reported recent use of prescription opioids (past 30 days) and 73.8% reported no use. Specifically, 14.3% of retired players reported
21	  opioid use only as prescribed, whereas 11.9% reported misuse (not prescribed or use other than as prescribed). Using prescription
22	  opioids to function while in the NFL was associated with any opioid use in the past 30 days [odds ratios (OR) 5 1.30, 95% CI: 1.12-
23	  1.50, P , 0.001]. Further, opioid use in the NFL to reduce stress and anxiety was associated with increased odds of past 30-day
24	  misuse of prescription opioids (OR 5 1.45, 95% CI: 1.01-2.11; P 5 0.048). Conclusions: The present study adds to the literature
25	  on elite athletes at high risk for pain and prescription opioid use and misuse. The findings may help to identify and provide early
26	  intervention for professional athletes most at risk for misuse of prescription opioids.
27	  Key Words: prescription opioids, drug use, athletes
28	  (Clin J Sport Med 2020;30:544–549)
