Reasons for Prescription Opioid Use While Playing
in the National Football League as Risk Factors for
Current Use and Misuse Among Former Players
Eugene M. Dunne, PhD,* Catherine W. Striley, PhD, MSW, MPE,† Zachary L. Mannes, MS,*
Breton M. Asken, MS, ATC,* Nicole Ennis, PhD,* and Linda B. Cottler, PhD, MPH, FACE†


  Abstract
  Objective: Prescription opioid misuse has become a significant public health issue. Previous research has examined predictors of
  prescription opioid use and misuse among former National Football League (NFL) players. The present study aimed to describe how
  reasons for prescription opioid use while in the NFL corresponds to use and misuse in retirement. Design: Former NFL players
  reporting prescription opioid use during their playing careers (N 5 336) were included in this secondary data analysis. Participants
  reported reasons for prescription opioid use, including pain management, use “to function,” to improve mood, to reduce stress, and
  to aid sleep. Results: Among retired NFL players with exposure to prescribed pain medication during their playing career, 26.2%
  reported recent use of prescription opioids (past 30 days) and 73.8% reported no use. Specifically, 14.3% of retired players reported
  opioid use only as prescribed, whereas 11.9% reported misuse (not prescribed or use other than as prescribed). Using prescription
  opioids to function while in the NFL was associated with any opioid use in the past 30 days [odds ratios (OR) 5 1.30, 95% CI: 1.12-
  1.50, P , 0.001]. Further, opioid use in the NFL to reduce stress and anxiety was associated with increased odds of past 30-day
  misuse of prescription opioids (OR 5 1.45, 95% CI: 1.01-2.11; P 5 0.048). Conclusions: The present study adds to the literature
  on elite athletes at high risk for pain and prescription opioid use and misuse. The findings may help to identify and provide early
  intervention for professional athletes most at risk for misuse of prescription opioids.
  Key Words: prescription opioids, drug use, athletes
  (Clin J Sport Med 2020;30:544–549)

  "abstract": "This secondary analysis examined whether the reasons former NFL players gave for prescription opioid use during their careers were linked to opioid use and misuse in retirement. Using opioids in the NFL to function was associated with any current use, and using them to reduce stress was associated with current misuse.",
  "tldr": "Among 336 former NFL players who had used prescription opioids in their careers, using them to function in the NFL was linked to any opioid use after retirement, and stress-relief use was linked to misuse. Sedative and risky alcohol use were common among current users, so screening should cover both.",
  "methods": "Secondary analysis of a telephone survey of retired NFL players conducted in 2010, restricted to the 336 players who had used prescription opioids during their careers (from a parent sample of 644). Players reported reasons for in-career use (to function, change mood, relax or relieve stress, sleep, pain), past-30-day use and misuse, and alcohol and sedative use. Logistic regression tested the reasons as predictors of any current use and of misuse versus use as prescribed, with pain use, alcohol and sedatives included in the models.",
  "findings": "Of the 336 players, 14.3% reported use only as prescribed and 11.9% reported misuse in the past 30 days. Use to function in the NFL was reported by 56.8% of current users and 28.2% of non-users (OR 1.30, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.50). Among current users, misusers were more likely than those using as prescribed to report stress-relief use in the NFL (35.0% vs 14.6%; OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.01 to 2.11) and risky drinking (32.5% vs 12.5%; OR 3.25, 95% CI 1.05 to 10.00).   "limitations": "The sample was restricted to former players who used opioids in the NFL and belong to the players' association, so it may overestimate health and underestimate substance use. The findings apply only to professional American football and to 'to function' as a broad category.",
  "practicalImplications": "Medical and team staff could ask players why they use opioids, with particular attention to use to function and to relieve stress, and screen current users for sedative and risky alcohol use. The authors recommend referral to evidence-based pain management for players with chronic pain or misuse.",
  "athleteDev": "Performance Application: Opioid use to function through injury was linked to later use, so staff who prescribe for players should ask why the medication is being taken and record those reasons alongside prescriptions. The study cannot show that changing practice reduces later misuse.",
  "rtp": "Return to Sport Application: The sample was retired players and the study did not measure return to play after injury, so it cannot inform return-to-sport decisions or opioid use during rehabilitation. It shows only that in-career reasons for use are associated with later use."

}
